title: EigenBench: Measuring Value Alignment Without Ground Truth
one_liner: When there is no right answer for what values a model should hold, use models judging each other to find which ones agree most.
lead: You want to know if a language model shares your values. But some values are subjective — no one has a clean right answer. EigenBench solves this by having a group of models judge each other's outputs, then tallying which models other models trust most, like a peer-review score. The result is a single honest number for each model showing how aligned it is to a value system.

problem.h2: Why you cannot simply grade value alignment
paras: When a model answers a question, we often know if it is factually right or wrong — we can check against reality. But when a model demonstrates a value like fairness or honesty, there is no objective ground truth to check against. Different people disagree on what counts as fair.

A beginner would try: pick some human raters, have them grade every model's outputs yes-or-no, and average the scores. This seems simple. But it breaks when raters themselves have different values. One rater might think a model is fair; another thinks it is not. Whose judgment do you trust?

callout.html: You need a score for each model's values, but no one agrees on what the right answer is, so you cannot just average human votes.

steps.text: Gather a group of language models and a written constitution (a description of the values you want to measure).
Each model answers the same scenario questions using the constitution as a guide, producing candidate outputs.
For each scenario, every model judges every other model's output: does this align to the constitution, yes or no?
Count up who said yes to whose outputs. Build a table of how often each model's judgment agreed with others.
Use a math method called EigenTrust to find which models are trustworthy judges, then use their votes to score each model's alignment.

paras: Instead of hiring human raters to score models on value alignment, EigenBench uses the models themselves as judges and lets their peer votes create the score. No human labels needed, because the models' judgments are the only ground truth you have.

hidden.name: trustworthiness of a model's judgment
paras: Trustworthiness is a single number for each model that says how much other models should trust this model's judgment when it evaluates alignment. A model with high trustworthiness is one whose yes-or-no votes agree with the votes of other trustworthy models.

The paper estimates trustworthiness by looking at the pattern of who agreed with whom. If a model's votes align with what other reliable models voted, that model's trustworthiness score rises. It is a recursive definition: you trust a model because other trusted models agree with it.

heat.caption: Darker means many other models agreed with this model's judgment. These are trustworthy judges.

reads.html: Trustworthiness measures whose opinion most models converge on. A model whose yes-or-no votes match other models' votes gets a high trustworthiness score.
EigenTrust computes an eigenvector (a stable pattern in how models vote for each other) where each model's score reflects weighted agreement with high-trustworthiness judges.

mechanism.h2: Why this finds honest consensus without labels
paras: Trustworthy judges do not need to agree with some external ground truth — they just need to agree with each other. If you have a group of models, the ones whose judgments most overlap are likely the ones making honest, thoughtful calls.

Here is the causal chain: When each model rates every other model's outputs, you get a table of yes-or-no votes. Now you rank which models are trustworthy by checking: whose votes did other trustworthy models also make? Models that voted the same way as other reliable judges get higher trustworthiness. Finally, to score each model's overall alignment, you take a weighted average of all the yes votes it received, but you weight each yes-vote by how trustworthy that judge is. Trustworthy judges' votes count more than unreliable ones. The result is a single alignment score for each model that reflects the consensus of the models the group trusts most.

Why does this work? Because there is a stable equilibrium: if most models have similar values, then the models whose judgments align with the group will be ranked as trustworthy, and their votes will reinforce their own high alignment scores. The system pulls toward a consensus without needing any external ground truth.

stages.s: Each model judges each output: align or not
Build judgment table: who agreed with whom

math.words: Each model's alignment score equals the weighted average of how often other models said its output was aligned, where each judge's weight is their trustworthiness score.
math.equation: alignment_j = sum_i ( trustworthiness_i * votes_i_to_j ) / sum_i trustworthiness_i
symbols: the alignment score for model j
how much you should trust judge i's opinion (computed from consensus)
fraction of yes-votes judge i gave to model j's outputs

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose four judges all rate model X.
Judge A (trustworthiness 0.8): said yes 90 percent of the time to X. Contribution: 0.8 * 0.9 = 0.72
Judge B (trustworthiness 0.6): said yes 70 percent of the time to X. Contribution: 0.6 * 0.7 = 0.42
Judge C (trustworthiness 0.3): said yes 50 percent of the time to X. Contribution: 0.3 * 0.5 = 0.15
Judge D (trustworthiness 0.3): said yes 30 percent of the time to X. Contribution: 0.3 * 0.3 = 0.09
Result: Model X aligns with the constitution 69 percent of the time, according to trustworthy judges.

math.note: Trusted judges' votes count more, so the final alignment score reflects the values of the models the ensemble agrees are most thoughtful.

charts.title: Human raters, average across all
charts.note: Averaging all human votes dilutes trusted raters with unreliable ones. The scores are close together and low overall.

charts.title: EigenBench with model judges
charts.note: Weighting by trustworthiness spreads the scores and lifts models with true value alignment. Clear ranking emerges.

items.b: All models have the same values.
items.html: If every model in the ensemble has nearly identical values, they will all agree with each other, and no model will stand out as more trustworthy. The method finds consensus, but the consensus might be narrow and not representative.

items.b: The constitution is vague or contradictory.
items.html: If the written value system has unclear rules, judges will disagree on interpretation, not because they have different values but because the spec is ambiguous. This noise breaks the trustworthiness signal.

items.b: Collusion or group-think in the ensemble.
items.html: If some models have been fine-tuned together or trained on the same data, they might have artificially similar judgments even if they are not correct. The trustworthiness computation will favor them falsely.

items.b: Done right: diverse ensemble, clear constitution.
items.html: When you have models with genuinely different training, and the constitution is specific and unambiguous, the trustworthiness scores stabilize, and the alignment rankings reflect real differences in values.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small ensemble of three to five language models. Write a simple, clear constitution describing one concrete value, like honesty (the model must not make up facts). Create ten scenarios where the models answer a question, and you can clearly see which answer is more honest. Have each model judge every other model's output against the constitution. Run the EigenBench algorithm: compute trustworthiness for each model based on agreement patterns, then compute each model's alignment score weighted by trustworthiness.
demo.metric_eq: Agreement with humans = number of times EigenBench ranking matches human ranking / total number of models
demo.closing: The demo succeeds when the EigenBench scores spread the models into a clear ranking that aligns with what a human would predict about their values, without ever showing the human judgments to the algorithm.
